extracted.intended_audience: advanced undergraduates, graduate students, and researchers learning/using category theory
extracted.subtask_description: Definitions, axioms, and basic constructions in category theory (small vs large categories, hom-sets, functors, duality, opposites, products, enriched and Ab-categories, concrete categories, hom-functors, and related examples).

rubrics_metrics.name: Small group / small set
rubrics_metrics.description: A small group is a small set with a group structure; concretely an ordered pair (U, m) where U is a small set and m: U x U -> U is a binary operation satisfying the usual group axioms. 'Small set' means a member of the chosen universe U (not 'small cardinality').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because small groups are elements of the universe U one can form the set of all small groups and homomorphisms between them to get the category Grp. Note: 'small' is relative to the chosen universe; e.g., {U} may be small as a set but not a 'small set' in this sense since {U} ∈ U would imply U ∈ U, contradicting regularity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Small category / large category
rubrics_metrics.description: A category is small if its set of objects and set of arrows are both small sets (members of the universe). A large category is one in which both the set of objects and the set of arrows are classes (proper or otherwise).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Set and Grp are not small (their object collections are not small sets); categories like Cis (category of all classes) or Cat' (category of all large categories) are not classes. The distinction matters for foundations and for forming categories of 'all' objects of a given type.

rubrics_metrics.name: Zermelo-Fraenkel axioms (assumed background)
rubrics_metrics.description: The text assumes standard Zermelo-Fraenkel axioms for set theory (membership relation ∈), including Extensionality, existence of the null set, existence of pairs {u,v}, ordered pairs (u,v), power set P(u), union ∪u, the axiom of infinity, the axiom of choice, the axiom of regularity, and the replacement axiom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These axioms are the assumed background so that the notion of a universe U and the manipulations of small sets and classes are meaningful; condition (v) in the universe definition corresponds to replacement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Replacement axiom (ZF)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a is a set and φ(x,y) is a functional property on a (for each x∈a there exists a unique y with φ(x,y)), then there exists a set consisting of all those y such that φ(x,y) holds for x∈a.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Informally: the image of a set a under a 'function' φ is a set. Replacement implies a form of comprehension used in the foundation; it is closely related to the universe condition (v).

rubrics_metrics.name: Universe U (Grothendieck-style universe conditions)
rubrics_metrics.description: A universe U is a set with closure properties (including closure under certain set-formation operations) so that members of U are called 'small sets'. Condition (v) corresponds to replacement; closure under products/unions can be used to replace some universe conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One-universe foundations suffice for many category-theory purposes. Exercises show, e.g., that if I: I -> U with each value in U and domain I∈U then products ∏_{i∈I} I_i ∈ U and unions ∪_{i∈I} I_i ∈ U, and that certain closure properties may replace condition (v). Grothendieck's stronger assumption (for every set X there is a universe U with X∈U) yields relative universes but still does not give a category of all groups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Class and proper class (Gödel-Bernays viewpoint)
rubrics_metrics.description: A class C is any subset C ⊆ U of the universe. Some classes (like U itself) are not small sets and are called proper classes. Small sets are also classes, but proper classes are not small.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using small sets and classes, many needed categories (Set, Grp, etc.) can be described; these are proper classes and thus large categories in this sense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Category definition via hom-sets (data i–v)
rubrics_metrics.description: A small category is given by: (i) a set of objects; (ii) a function assigning to each ordered pair (a,b) a set hom(a,b); (iii) for each triple (a,b,c) a composition function hom(b,c) x hom(a,b) -> hom(a,c); (iv) for each object b an identity element 1_b ∈ hom(b,b); and (v) a disjointness axiom: if (a,b) ≠ (a',b') then hom(a,b) ∩ hom(a',b') = ∅. The usual associativity and unit axioms must hold.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This hom-set formulation is equivalent to the original object/arrow definition. Axiom (v) ensures each arrow has a definite domain and codomain; if it fails one can 'label' hom-sets (e.g., replace hom(a,b) by {a}×hom(a,b)×{b}). Some authors omit axiom (v).

rubrics_metrics.name: Associativity and unit axioms (category)
rubrics_metrics.description: Composition must be associative and identities act as units: for composable arrows f,g,h the equality (h∘g)∘f = h∘(g∘f) holds, and for each f: a->b one has 1_b ∘ f = f = f ∘ 1_a.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are the 'familiar' axioms referenced in the hom-set data; they can be expressed either equationally or by commutative diagrams.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disjointness axiom for hom-sets
rubrics_metrics.description: If (a,b) ≠ (a',b') then hom(a,b) ∩ hom(a',b') = ∅ (so distinct hom-sets are disjoint).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Included to guarantee arrows have definite domain and codomain; if omitted authors sometimes adjust hom-sets by labeling to restore disjointness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functor (hom-set formulation)
rubrics_metrics.description: A functor T: C -> B consists of the object function together with functions φ_{e,e'}: C(e,e') -> B(Te,Te') (sending f ↦ Tf) such that φ_{e,e'}(1_e) = 1_{Te} and such that diagrams expressing preservation of composition commute (i.e., T(g∘f) = Tg ∘ Tf).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the usual requirement that functors preserve identities and composition; the hom-set viewpoint explicitly exhibits the maps on hom-sets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural transformation (hom-set hint)
rubrics_metrics.description: A natural transformation η: S ⇒ T (between functors S,T: C -> B) may be described in terms of functions C(e,e') -> B(Se,Te'), mapping arrows to components that satisfy the naturality commuting conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text leaves the full description to the reader but indicates the hom-set perspective: naturality means certain diagrams/functions commute for each arrow in C.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concrete category (faithful forgetful functor)
rubrics_metrics.description: A concrete category is a pair (C, U) where C is a category and U: C -> Set a faithful functor. Under U, each object c has an underlying set Uc, and each arrow f: b->c corresponds to the actual function U f: U b -> U c; composition of arrows corresponds to composition of functions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many large categories described (Ab, R-Mod, Mod-R, etc.) are concrete relative to evident forgetful functors; some (Toph, Rei) are not concrete in this sense. Faithfulness lets one identify arrows with underlying functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ab-category / preadditive category
rubrics_metrics.description: An Ab-category (preadditive category) A is a category in which each hom-set A(a,b) is an additive abelian group and composition is bilinear: (g+g')∘(f+f') = g∘f + g∘f' + g'∘f + g'∘f'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equivalently composition is a bilinear map A(b,c) × A(a,b) -> A(a,c), which can be expressed as a linear map A(b,c) ⊗ A(a,b) -> A(a,c). Examples: Ab, R-Mod, Mod-R. The Ab-category structure may be generalized to categories enriched in other monoidal categories (enriched categories).

rubrics_metrics.name: Additive functor
rubrics_metrics.description: If A and B are Ab-categories, a functor T: A -> B is additive when each induced function T: A(a,a') -> B(Ta,Ta') is a homomorphism of abelian groups, i.e., T(f+f') = Tf + Tf'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The composite of additive functors is additive. Additive functors are the arrows in the category Ab-cat of small Ab-categories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Set* and pointed categories (basepoint-preserving maps)
rubrics_metrics.description: Set* is the category of small pointed sets: objects are nonempty sets with a designated base point *; morphisms f: P -> Q are functions sending basepoint to basepoint (f(*_P) = *_Q). Similarly Top* is the category of small pointed topological spaces with base-point-preserving continuous maps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In Set* the one-point set {*} is both initial and terminal. In Set* a morphism is monic iff it has a left inverse, epi iff it has a right inverse, and invertible iff both. In homotopy-theoretic variants (Toph*, Toph) homotopies must preserve basepoints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Category Rei of binary relations
rubrics_metrics.description: Objects: small sets X,Y,...; arrows R: X -> Y are binary relations R ⊆ X × Y. Composition S ∘ R is the usual relational (relative) product: {(x,z) | ∃y with (x,y)∈R and (y,z)∈S}. Identity on X is the identity relation. Rei contains Set as a subcategory where functions are viewed as relations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rei has additional structure: each relation R has a converse R*: Y -> X of reversed pairs. Rei is not concrete in the sense of all arrows being functions. This example shows arrows in a category need not be functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Toph and homotopy categories (arrows as homotopy classes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Toph: objects are small topological spaces; morphisms are homotopy classes of continuous maps. Composition is composition of homotopy classes. In Toph the homotopy class of an injection need not be monic (e.g., inclusion of circle into disk).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This illustrates that being an arrow need not coincide with being a function; homotopy classes can lose injectivity or other pointwise properties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duality principle (reverse all arrows)
rubrics_metrics.description: The dual of a statement of the elementary theory of an abstract category is formed by replacing 'domain'↔'codomain' and reversing composites (h is composite of g with f ↔ h is composite of f with g), leaving logical connectives unchanged. If a statement is a consequence of the axioms, its dual is also a consequence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Duality gives immediate dual theorems (e.g., uniqueness of terminal object up to iso gives uniqueness of initial object up to iso). The dual of the dual is the original statement. Duality also applies to theories involving several categories and functors (reverse arrows in each category but not the functors).

rubrics_metrics.name: Opposite category C^op
rubrics_metrics.description: C^op has the same objects as C but arrows f^op: b->a corresponding one-to-one to arrows f: a->b in C, with composition defined so f^op ∘ g^op = (g ∘ f)^op. Monics in C^op correspond to epis in C, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This realizes the duality principle concretely: a sentence L is true in C^op iff the dual sentence L* is true in C. Functors T: C->B induce TOP: C^op -> B^op etc.; the assignment C ↦ C^op, T ↦ T^op is a covariant functor Cat -> Cat.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contravariant functor (as covariant from opposite)
rubrics_metrics.description: A contravariant functor S on C to B assigns to each object c ∈ C an object Sc ∈ B and to each arrow f: a->b an arrow Sf: Sb->Sa in B, such that S(f ∘ g) = (Sg) ∘ (Sf) (order of composition is inverted). Equivalently, S is a covariant functor C^op -> B.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: power-set functor P: Set -> Set (P(f): P(Y)->P(X) is inverse image f^{-1}), dual vector-space functor V -> V* mapping f to f* : W*->V*. Contravariant functors are often represented as covariant functors from opposites for convenience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hom-functors (covariant and contravariant)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a category C with small hom-sets, for each object a the covariant hom-functor C(a,-): C -> Set sends b↦hom(a,b) and k:b->b' to hom(a,k): hom(a,b)->hom(a,b') by f ↦ k∘f. Dually, for each b the contravariant hom-functor C(-,b): C^op -> Set sends a↦hom(a,b) and g:a->a' to hom(g,b): hom(a',b)->hom(a,b) by f ↦ f∘g.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notation: hom(a,b) = C(a,b) etc.; hom(a,k) sometimes written k_* (composition on left) and hom(g,b) written g^* (composition on right). Diagrams expressing naturality/commutativity (k_* and g^* commuting) hold. If hom-sets are not small, choose a sufficiently large receiving category Ens = Set_V to host them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enriched categories (hom-objects in a monoidal category)
rubrics_metrics.description: A generalization where hom-sets are replaced by hom-objects in a category like Ab equipped with a multiplication (tensor) and unit; composition is given by a morphism A(b,c) ⊗ A(a,b) -> A(a,c) and units by Z -> A(a,a).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ab-categories are the simplest example (enrichment over Ab). See Kelly [1982] for general theory. Enriched categories permit describing categories where hom-structures carry extra algebraic structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Product of categories B × C (construction and universal property)
rubrics_metrics.description: Objects: pairs (b,c). Arrows: pairs (f,g) where f: b->b' in B and g: c->c' in C. Composition defined componentwise: (f',g')∘(f,g) = (f'∘f, g'∘g). Projections P: B×C -> B and Q: B×C -> C defined by P(b,c)=b, Q(b,c)=c.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Universal property: given any D and functors R: D->B and T: D->C there is a unique functor F: D->B×C with P∘F = R and Q∘F = T (F(h) = (R(h), T(h))). Product extends to functors: given U: B->B' and V: C->C' there is U×V: B×C -> B'×C' defined componentwise. The product operation is itself functorial (x: Cat×Cat -> Cat).

rubrics_metrics.name: Bifunctor (functor of two variables) and determination by fixed-argument functors
rubrics_metrics.description: A functor S: B×C -> D is a bifunctor. Fixing one argument yields ordinary functors S(-,c): B->D and S(b,-): C->D. Conversely, given functors L_c: B->D for each c and M_b: C->D for each b with the agreement M_b(c) = L_c(b) for all b,c, there exists a bifunctor S with S(-,c)=L_c and S(b,-)=M_b iff for every pair of arrows f: b->b' in B and g: c->c' in C the obvious compatibility equality in D holds (the two ways of composing values agree); these common composites define S(f,g).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicit compatibility (diagrammatic) condition: for all f,g the two arrows L_{c'}(f) ∘ M_b(g) and M_{b'}(g) ∘ L_c(f) in D must be equal; when they are, that common arrow is S(f,g). Bifunctors include cartesian product ×: Set×Set -> Set.

rubrics_metrics.name: Product functor behavior and bifunctor examples
rubrics_metrics.description: Product of functors: (U×V)(b,c) = (U b, V c) and on arrows (U×V)(f,g) = (U f, V g). Bifunctors such as the cartesian product X×Y: Set×Set -> Set arise naturally and fixing one variable gives ordinary functors of the other variable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proposition and examples show how bifunctors are assembled from one-variable functors and the necessary commutation condition for arrows.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples linking categorical notions to concrete properties (monic/epi/invertible)
rubrics_metrics.description: In many concrete categories: monic arrows correspond to injective maps, epi to surjective maps, invertible to bijections (e.g., Ab, R-Mod, Top). However, there are important exceptions and nuances (e.g., in the category of rings, inclusions like Z→Q can be epi as arrows without being surjective; in homotopy categories an injection's homotopy class need not be monic).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The examples illustrate that categorical properties (monic, epi, iso) should be checked in the categorical sense, not assumed to coincide with pointwise function properties in every context. Use counterexamples (Z→Q, inclusion circle→disk in homotopy) as cautionary notes.
